entities.name: Andrea da Segni
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andrea dei Conti di Segni (died February 1, 1302) emerged from the powerful Roman noble family of Conti di Segni, a lineage that profoundly influenced the medieval Papacy, producing figures like Pope Innocent III and Pope Gregory IX. Renouncing the worldly prestige of his birthright, Andrea embraced the rigorous asceticism of the Franciscan Order, becoming a revered figure whose life exemplified the ideals of poverty, humility, and devout service in late 13th-century Italy. His spiritual authority and reputation for sanctity made him a significant, albeit quiet, force in shaping the Franciscan charism during a period of intense internal debate and external challenges for the burgeoning order.

After joining the Friars Minor, Andrea dedicated himself to a life of contemplation and rigorous penance, often withdrawing to hermitages for prayer while also engaging in acts of charity. He reportedly performed numerous miracles, including healing the sick and predicting future events, which contributed significantly to his veneration among the populace. Unlike many of his noble relatives who pursued ecclesiastical power, Andrea deliberately chose a path of radical self-abnegation, living in austere conditions and serving the poor, thereby embodying the foundational spirit of Saint Francis himself. His cousin, Pope Alexander IV (Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni), held him in high esteem, often seeking his spiritual counsel, a testament to Andrea's perceived holiness.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrea da Segni's life exemplified the spiritual ideals of the Franciscan Order in 13th-century Italy, influencing the piety of friars and lay faithful. His veneration as a Blessed established a local pilgrimage site and reinforced the order's core values.
